question: Where are the Hazardous Materials Regulations (HMR) found, and which federal agency issues them?
choice_a: Title 29 of the Code of Federal Regulations, issued by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration
choice_b: Title 49, Parts 171-180, issued by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration
choice_c: Title 49 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Parts 171-180, issued by the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA)
choice_d: Title 18 of the U.S. Code, issued by the Environmental Protection Agency
explanation: The manual states the Hazardous Materials Regulations (HMR) are found in Title 49 CFR, Parts 171 through 180, commonly cited as 49 CFR 171-180, and are issued by PHMSA, part of the U.S. Department of Transportation.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, Introduction

question: What must a driver have before transporting hazardous material as defined in 49 CFR 383.5?
choice_a: A CDL with a hazardous materials endorsement, obtained by passing a written test on the regulations and requirements
choice_b: Only a letter of authorization from the shipper
choice_c: A standard Class D driver's license with no additional endorsement
choice_d: A commercial learner's permit is sufficient with no further testing
explanation: The manual states you must have a CDL with a hazardous materials endorsement before driving any vehicle to transport hazardous material as defined in 49 CFR 383.5, obtained by passing a written test.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, Introduction

question: How long must hazardous materials employers keep a record of training for each employee?
choice_a: As long as the employee works with hazardous materials, and for 90 days after
choice_b: Indefinitely, with no expiration on the retention requirement
choice_c: Only until the employee's next annual performance review
choice_d: Only for 30 days after the training is completed
explanation: The manual states hazardous materials employers are required to keep a record of training for each employee as long as that employee is working with hazardous materials, and for 90 days after.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, Introduction

question: How often do the regulations require people working with hazardous materials to be trained and tested?
choice_a: At least once every year
choice_b: At least once every five years
choice_c: Only once, at the start of employment
choice_d: At least once every three years
explanation: The manual states the regulations require people working with hazardous materials to be trained and tested at least once every three years.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, Introduction

question: What must the shipper do regarding a hazardous materials shipment, according to the manual?
choice_a: Package, mark, and label the materials; prepare shipping papers; provide emergency response information; and supply placards
choice_b: Only pay for the fuel used during transport
choice_c: Only determine the delivery route the driver must take
choice_d: Only load the vehicle; all other duties belong to the driver
explanation: The manual states the shipper must package, mark, and label the materials, prepare shipping papers, provide emergency response information, and supply placards.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.2.1 The Shipper

question: What must a carrier do before transportation of a hazardous materials shipment, according to the manual?
choice_a: Notify the destination facility of the shipment's arrival time only
choice_b: Repackage all hazardous materials shipments regardless of shipper preparation
choice_c: Only verify the driver has a valid license, without checking the shipment itself
choice_d: Check that the shipper correctly described, marked, labeled, and otherwise prepared the shipment, and refuse improper shipments
explanation: The manual states the carrier takes the shipment from the shipper to its destination, checks before transportation that the shipper correctly prepared the shipment, and refuses improper shipments.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.2.2 The Carrier

question: Which of the following is listed as a driver's responsibility when transporting hazardous materials?
choice_a: Set the price charged for transporting the hazardous material
choice_b: Repackage improperly labeled shipments personally before departure
choice_c: Determine the hazard class of the material without shipper input
choice_d: Refuse leaking packages and shipments, and report accidents/incidents involving hazardous materials to the right government agency
explanation: The manual lists driver responsibilities including refusing leaking packages and shipments, and reporting accidents/incidents to the right government agency when they occur while the driver is in physical control of the shipment.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.2.3 The Driver

question: How many different hazard classes does a material's hazard class reflect, according to the manual's Hazardous Materials Class Chart?
choice_a: Nine
choice_b: Seven
choice_c: Twelve
choice_d: Five
explanation: The manual states there are nine different hazard classes, with the types of materials included shown in Figure 9.1, the Hazardous Materials Class Chart.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.1 Definitions

question: According to the Hazardous Materials Class Chart, how are Divisions 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3 categorized?
choice_a: All Class 2 divisions represent flammable liquids, not gases
choice_b: 2.1 Flammable Gases (example: Propane), 2.2 Non-Flammable Gases (example: Helium), 2.3 Poisonous/Toxic Gases (example: Fluorine, Compressed)
choice_c: 2.1 Corrosive Gases, 2.2 Radioactive Gases, 2.3 Explosive Gases
choice_d: 2.1 Non-Flammable Gases, 2.2 Flammable Gases, 2.3 Infectious Gases
explanation: The manual's class chart lists Division 2.1 as Flammable Gases (Propane), 2.2 as Non-Flammable Gases (Helium), and 2.3 as Poisonous/Toxic Gases (Fluorine, Compressed).
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, Figure 9.1 Hazardous Materials Class Chart

question: According to the class chart, which class covers Corrosive materials (example: Battery Fluid) and which covers Radioactive materials (example: Uranium)?
choice_a: Class 5 covers Corrosive materials; Class 8 covers Radioactive materials
choice_b: Class 9 covers Corrosive materials; Class 6 covers Radioactive materials
choice_c: Class 8 covers Corrosive materials; Class 7 covers Radioactive materials
choice_d: Class 6 covers Corrosive materials; Class 9 covers Radioactive materials
explanation: The manual's class chart lists Class 8 as Corrosive (Battery Fluid) and Class 7 as Radioactive (Uranium).
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, Figure 9.1 Hazardous Materials Class Chart

question: Where must a driver keep hazardous materials shipping papers while driving?
choice_a: In the sleeper berth, out of the driver's reach
choice_b: In a pouch on the driver's door, or in clear view within immediate reach while the seat belt is fastened
choice_c: Locked in the glove compartment at all times
choice_d: Mailed electronically to the destination facility instead of carried physically
explanation: The manual requires drivers to keep hazardous materials shipping papers in a pouch on the driver's door, or in clear view within immediate reach while the seat belt is fastened while driving, or on the driver's seat when out of the vehicle.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.1 Definitions

question: How many identical placards must a placarded vehicle have, and where are they placed?
choice_a: Exactly two placards, on the front and rear only
choice_b: At least four identical placards, on the front, rear, and both sides of the vehicle
choice_c: At least four placards, but each may show a different hazard class
choice_d: Only one placard, mounted on the roof of the vehicle
explanation: The manual states a placarded vehicle must have at least four identical placards, placed on the front, rear, and both sides of the vehicle.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: What are hazardous materials identification numbers, and what letters typically precede them?
choice_a: A two-letter code with no numeric component
choice_b: A code that is unique to each individual shipment, never reused
choice_c: A four-digit code used by first responders to identify hazardous materials, preceded by the letters 'NA' or 'UN'
choice_d: A six-digit code preceded by the letters 'DOT'
explanation: The manual states identification numbers are a four-digit code used by first responders to identify hazardous materials, and the letters 'NA' or 'UN' precede the identification number.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: What are the three main lists shippers, carriers, and drivers use to identify hazardous materials?
choice_a: Only the Hazardous Materials Table, with no appendices used
choice_b: The IRS tax code, the DOT vehicle registration list, and the EPA emissions list
choice_c: The FMCSA driver qualification list, the ERG, and the state highway map
choice_d: The Hazardous Materials Table (172.101), Appendix A (Hazardous Substances and Reportable Quantities), and Appendix B (List of Marine Pollutants)
explanation: The manual states the three main lists are Section 172.101 (the Hazardous Materials Table), Appendix A to 172.101 (List of Hazardous Substances and Reportable Quantities), and Appendix B to 172.101 (List of Marine Pollutants).
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: What does an entry of 'Forbidden' in Column 3 (Hazard Class or Division) of the Hazardous Materials Table mean?
choice_a: The material must never be transported
choice_b: The material is exempt from all placarding requirements
choice_c: The material requires a special permit before an otherwise-normal shipment
choice_d: The material may only be transported by air, never by highway
explanation: The manual states Column 3 shows a material's hazard class or division, or the entry 'Forbidden,' and instructs to never transport a 'Forbidden' material.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: What three things must you know to decide which placards to use for a hazmat shipment?
choice_a: The destination state, the day of the week, and the current fuel price
choice_b: Only the material's color and its physical state (solid, liquid, or gas)
choice_c: The shipper's business address, the driver's years of experience, and the vehicle's model year
choice_d: The material's hazard class, the amount being shipped, and the amount of all hazardous materials of all classes on your vehicle
explanation: The manual states you can decide which placards to use if you know the material's hazard class, the amount being shipped, and the amount of all hazardous materials of all classes on your vehicle.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: If the words INHALATION HAZARD appear on the shipping paper or package, what does the manual require?
choice_a: No placard is required if the shipment is under 1,000 pounds
choice_b: Display of the POISON INHALATION HAZARD or POISON GAS placard in addition to other placards required by the product's hazard class
choice_c: Only the standard hazard class placard is needed, with no additional placard
choice_d: The shipment must travel only at night to reduce public exposure
explanation: The manual states that if INHALATION HAZARD appears on the shipping paper or package, the rules require display of the POISON INHALATION HAZARD or POISON GAS placards, in addition to other placards required by the product's hazard class, and the 1,000 pound exception does not apply.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.3 Lists of Regulated Products / 9.3.11 Placard Tables

question: What marking must bulk packages of a Marine Pollutant display, and is it considered a placard?
choice_a: A blue diamond with the letters 'MP,' which replaces all other placards
choice_b: No special marking is required beyond the standard hazard class placard
choice_c: A red circle with a skull and crossbones, which counts as an official placard
choice_d: A white triangle with a fish and an 'X' through the fish; this marking is not a placard but must be displayed on the outside of the vehicle
explanation: The manual states any bulk package of a Marine Pollutant must display a white triangle with a fish and an X through it; this marking is not a placard but must also be displayed on the outside of the vehicle, with a shipping paper notation of 'Marine Pollutant.'
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.3 Appendix B to 49 CFR 172.101

question: When a shipping paper lists both hazardous and non-hazardous cargo, how must the hazardous materials be identified?
choice_a: Listed last, in the same color as non-hazardous items
choice_b: Only noted verbally to the receiving warehouse
choice_c: Marked with a checkmark in a column labeled 'Misc'
choice_d: Entered first, highlighted in a contrasting color, OR identified by an 'X' before the shipping description in a column captioned 'HM'
explanation: The manual states hazardous materials must be entered first, highlighted in a contrasting color, or identified by an X placed before the shipping description in a column captioned 'HM' (or RQ, if a reportable quantity needs to be identified).
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.5 The Item Description

question: In what order must the basic description of a hazardous material appear on a shipping paper?
choice_a: Packing group, hazard class, shipping name, then identification number
choice_b: Identification number, proper shipping name, hazard class or division, and the packing group (if any)
choice_c: The order does not matter as long as all elements are present somewhere on the page
choice_d: Shipper's name, then hazard class, then destination address
explanation: The manual states the basic description includes the identification number, proper shipping name, hazard class or division, and the packing group, if any, in that order.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.5 The Item Description

question: How long must shippers keep a copy of shipping papers for hazardous waste, compared to other hazardous materials?
choice_a: 1 year for hazardous waste, versus 3 years for other hazardous materials
choice_b: 3 years for hazardous waste, versus 2 years for other hazardous materials, after the initial carrier accepts the material
choice_c: The retention period is identical for both at 10 years
choice_d: Hazardous waste shipping papers need not be retained at all
explanation: The manual states shippers must keep a copy of shipping papers for 2 years after the initial carrier accepts the material, but must keep hazardous waste shipping papers for 3 years.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.5 The Item Description

question: What must a driver do when transporting hazardous waste, regarding the Uniform Hazardous Waste Manifest?
choice_a: Sign and carry it, and only give the waste shipment to another registered carrier or disposal/treatment facility
choice_b: It is optional and only required for waste transported by rail
choice_c: The driver need not sign it, only the shipper needs to sign
choice_d: The manifest replaces the need for any placards on the vehicle
explanation: The manual states that when transporting hazardous waste, you must sign and carry a Uniform Hazardous Waste Manifest, and may only give the waste shipment to another registered carrier or disposal/treatment facility.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.9 Hazardous Waste Manifest

question: Under what circumstance are you allowed to move a vehicle that is improperly placarded?
choice_a: Anytime, as long as the trip is less than one mile
choice_b: Only during an emergency, in order to protect life or property
choice_c: Never, under any circumstance whatsoever
choice_d: Anytime, as long as the vehicle stays under the posted speed limit
explanation: The manual states you are only allowed to move an improperly placarded vehicle during an emergency, in order to protect life or property.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.10 Placarding

question: According to the manual's Placard Table 1, which materials must be placarded whenever any amount is transported?
choice_a: Materials such as 1.1 Mass Explosives, 2.3 Poisonous/Toxic Gases, and 4.3 Dangerous When Wet
choice_b: No hazard class requires placarding for any amount; all require the 1,001-pound threshold
choice_c: Only ORM-D materials
choice_d: Only Class 9 Miscellaneous Hazardous Materials
explanation: The manual's Table 1 (Any Amount) lists categories such as 1.1 Mass Explosives, 2.3 Poisonous/Toxic Gases, and 4.3 Dangerous When Wet as requiring placarding whenever any amount is transported.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.11 Placard Table 1

question: Except for bulk packaging, when do Table 2 hazard classes need placards, according to the manual?
choice_a: Table 2 materials never require placarding regardless of quantity
choice_b: Only if the total amount exceeds 5,000 pounds
choice_c: Any amount whatsoever, with no minimum threshold
choice_d: Only if the total amount transported is 1,001 pounds or more, including the package, added across all shipping papers
explanation: The manual states that except for bulk packaging, Table 2 hazard classes need placards only if the total amount transported is 1,001 pounds or more including the package, adding amounts from all shipping papers for all Table 2 products on board.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.11 Placard Table 2

question: Under what conditions may a driver use a DANGEROUS placard instead of separate placards for each Table 2 hazard class?
choice_a: When 1,001 pounds or more of two or more Table 2 hazard classes requiring different placards are on board, and no single Table 2 class reaches 2,205 pounds or more at any one place
choice_b: Whenever the driver prefers not to display specific hazard class placards
choice_c: The DANGEROUS placard is mandatory whenever any hazardous material is on board
choice_d: Only when transporting Class 1 explosives exclusively
explanation: The manual states the DANGEROUS placard may be used instead of separate Table 2 placards when you have 1,001 pounds or more of two or more Table 2 hazard classes requiring different placards, and you have not loaded 2,205 pounds or more of any single Table 2 class at one place; it is an option, not a requirement.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.11 Placard Tables

question: Does a bulk package containing only the residue of a hazardous material need to be placarded?
choice_a: Only if the bulk package is being transported internationally
choice_b: Yes, a bulk package and the vehicle transporting it must be placarded even if it only has the residue of a hazardous material
choice_c: Only if the residue weighs more than 1,001 pounds
choice_d: No, residue-only bulk packages are exempt from all placarding
explanation: The manual states a bulk package, and a vehicle transporting a bulk package, must be placarded even if it only has the residue of a hazardous material.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.3.11 Placard Tables

question: Near which hazard classes must smoking never occur during loading or unloading, according to the manual?
choice_a: Smoking restrictions apply only to Class 7 (Radioactive) materials
choice_b: Only Class 8 (Corrosives)
choice_c: Class 1 (Explosives), 2.1 (Flammable Gas), 3 (Flammable Liquids), 4 (Flammable Solids), and 5 (Oxidizers)
choice_d: Only Class 9 (Miscellaneous Hazardous Materials)
explanation: The manual states you should never smoke around Class 1 (Explosives), 2.1 (Flammable Gas), 3 (Flammable Liquids), 4 (Flammable Solids), and 5 (Oxidizers) when loading or unloading.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.4.1 No Smoking

question: What does the manual say about transferring hazardous materials from one package to another while in transit?
choice_a: Transferring is allowed for any package as long as gloves are worn
choice_b: Transferring is only prohibited for Class 1 explosives
choice_c: Never transfer hazardous materials from one package to another while in transit, though you may empty a cargo tank
choice_d: Transferring is allowed as long as it happens at a rest stop
explanation: The manual states that after loading, you should never open any package during your trip or transfer hazardous materials from one package to another while in transit; you may empty a cargo tank, but not any other package while it is on the vehicle.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.4.1 Secure Against Movement

question: For which hazard classes does the manual say cargo heaters, including automatic cargo heater/air conditioner units, are usually forbidden?
choice_a: Class 9 (Miscellaneous) only
choice_b: Class 6 (Poison) and Class 8 (Corrosive) only
choice_c: Class 1 (Explosives), Class 2.1 (Flammable Gas), and Class 3 (Flammable Liquids)
choice_d: All hazard classes are permitted with cargo heaters as long as the heater is off during loading
explanation: The manual states there are special cargo heater rules for loading Class 1 (Explosives), Class 2.1 (Flammable Gas), and Class 3 (Flammable Liquids), and the rules usually forbid use of cargo heaters for these products.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.4.1 Cargo Heater Rules

question: Which hazard classes cannot be transported as overhang or tailgate loads and generally must be in a closed cargo space?
choice_a: Class 6 (Poison) and Class 7 (Radioactive) only
choice_b: Class 3 (Flammable Liquids) only
choice_c: Class 1 (Explosives), Class 4 (Flammable Solids), and Class 5 (Oxidizers)
choice_d: Class 2 (Compressed Gases) and Class 9 (Miscellaneous) only
explanation: The manual states you can't have overhang or tailgate loads of Class 1 (Explosives), Class 4 (Flammable Solids), and Class 5 (Oxidizers); these must be loaded into a closed cargo space unless packages are fire- and water-resistant or covered with a fire- and water-resistant tarp.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.4.1 Use Closed Cargo Space

question: What must a driver do before loading or unloading explosives (Class 1)?
choice_a: Turn the engine off, then check the cargo space, disabling cargo heaters and checking for sharp points that might damage cargo
choice_b: Only check the cargo space after loading is already complete
choice_c: Leave the engine running to power the loading equipment
choice_d: Only the shipper, never the driver, is responsible for these checks
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to turn the engine off before loading or unloading explosives, then check the cargo space, disable cargo heaters, and look for sharp points such as bolts, screws, nails, or broken panels that might damage cargo.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.4.2 Class 1 (Explosives) Materials

question: If a vehicle doesn't have racks to hold cylinders of compressed gas, what must be true of the cargo space floor, and how must cylinders be held?
choice_a: The floor must be flat, and cylinders must be held upright, in racks attached to the vehicle, or in boxes that will keep them from turning over
choice_b: The floor may be uneven as long as cylinders are wrapped in blankets
choice_c: There are no special floor or positioning requirements for compressed gas cylinders
choice_d: Cylinders must always be loaded lying down regardless of racks
explanation: The manual states that without racks, the cargo space floor must be flat, and cylinders must be held upright, in racks attached to the vehicle, or in boxes that will keep them from turning over.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.4.2 Class 2 (Compressed Gases)

question: Where must a package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD never be loaded?
choice_a: In the rear-most compartment of any trailer
choice_b: There are no restrictions as long as the package is properly labeled
choice_c: In the driver's cab or sleeper, or with food material for human or animal consumption
choice_d: Anywhere other than directly behind the fifth wheel
explanation: The manual states you must never load a package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD in the driver's cab or sleeper, or with food material for human or animal consumption.
source_note: Maryland Commercial Driver's License Manual (DL-151, 05/26), Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MDOT MVA) -- Section 9, 9.4.2 Division 2.3 or 6.1 Materials
